summary:
## OECD Growth Upgrade

Korea's first quarter economic growth has been recognized as the highest among OECD nations, prompting international attention and investor confidence. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development significantly upgraded Korea's full-year growth forecast from 1.7% to 2.6%, reflecting improved economic momentum driven by robust semiconductor exports and strong trade performance. This upgrade demonstrates the resilience of Korea's economy despite global uncertainties, and government officials are actively promoting these achievements in international markets to attract foreign investment.

## Europe Investment Roadshow

Vice Minister Heo Jang conducted an investor presentation in Paris at the OECD Korean representation, targeting major European asset managers including Amundi and BNP Paribas. The roadshow highlighted Korea's top OECD growth rate, robust export performance, and consecutive current account surpluses as investment attractions. Officials also promoted plans for 24-hour market operations and offshore Korean won settlement systems to enhance Korea's appeal as a financial hub. The government successfully issued 3 billion dollars of foreign currency-denominated stabilization bonds at record-low spreads out of the 5 billion dollar annual issuance limit, with decisions on the remaining 2 billion dollars to be made based on international financial market conditions.

## Current Account Surplus Record

Korea's current account showed remarkable strength in April, posting a surplus of 28.29 billion dollars, marking the second-highest monthly figure on record. The cumulative current account surplus for January through April reached 102.67 billion dollars, the highest level ever recorded in any four-month period. The merchandise trade balance contributed 33.38 billion dollars to this surplus, also representing the second-highest monthly result. This exceptional performance reflects Korea's competitive advantage in semiconductor exports and overall manufacturing strength, though it ironically coincides with currency pressures affecting domestic economic conditions.

## Won Weakening Amid Surplus Paradox

Despite three consecutive years of current account surpluses, the Korean won has depreciated to its weakest level since the 2009 global financial crisis, approaching the 1,550 won-per-dollar level. The currency weakness stems from foreign investor outflows, with overseas investors executing net selling worth approximately 2.5 trillion won across both KOSPI and KOSDAQ markets. Inflation pressure and expectations of US interest rate increases have exacerbated capital outflows, creating headwinds for domestic demand and household budgets as government support payments lose value through currency depreciation. This phenomenon highlights the complex relationship between trade surpluses and currency movements in modern global finance.

## Stock Market Turmoil

The KOSPI index plummeted sharply, triggering a selling-side circuit breaker at 9:08 AM after declining 5.20%, with the index at 1,309.56 points. The KOSDAQ index also experienced significant losses, briefly breaking below the 1,000-point level during intraday trading. Semiconductor-related stocks led the decline following an approximately 12% selloff in Broadcom on US markets, spreading weakness throughout the Korean technology sector. Program selling pressure combined with foreign investor withdrawals created a perfect storm, with the KOSPI experiencing its tenth circuit breaker activation of the year.

## Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Push

The government is accelerating a 400-billion-won advanced data center project in Jangseong, Jeollanam-do, recognized as a strategic AI forward base for the nation. To expedite construction, authorities are applying a fast-track exemption from local budget investment reviews, targeting completion by 2027 and operational launch by 2028. This mega-project represents the seventh initiative under the Regional Revitalization Investment Fund, positioning Korea to strengthen its AI infrastructure and compete globally in the emerging data center industry. The project received explicit support from Deputy Prime Minister Goo Yun-chul, underscoring its importance to national economic strategy.

## Real Estate Market Stress

Seoul faces serious housing challenges as jeonse deposits plummeted 28.7% compared to last year, with available deposits dropping to 18,455 units from 25,886 units. Apartment jeonse prices have surged dramatically, creating affordability crises particularly in Nowon, Dobong, Gangbuk, and Songbuk districts, where prices increased 8.8% year-to-date. Demand has shifted toward officetels, with jeonse transactions rising 9.1% to 34,278 units in the first four months of 2026. Mayor-elect Oh Se-hoon identified the real estate crisis as Seoul's primary challenge, warning of potential disaster without policy direction changes.

## Debt Improvement Trajectory

Korea's government debt-to-GDP ratio received positive revisions from OECD economists, with 2026 estimates lowered from 52.0% to 48.2%, and 2027 projections reduced from 55.0% to 50.2%. These substantial downward revisions reflect improved fiscal sustainability through productive government spending that supports economic growth. Finance Minister Goo emphasized the positive feedback loop between fiscal policy and economic expansion, noting that stronger growth translates into improved debt dynamics and long-term fiscal stability.

## Export-Oriented Industries Benefit

Industries heavily dependent on exports, including semiconductors, shipbuilding, and defense manufacturing, stand to benefit from won depreciation as their products become more price-competitive internationally. Conversely, industries requiring significant raw material imports—including aviation, petrochemicals, and steel—face rising production costs that squeeze profit margins. This sectoral divergence creates winners and losers within Korea's economy, with the currency movement accentuating underlying economic structural differences.

## Investor Implications

The current economic environment presents mixed signals requiring careful navigation. While Korea's exceptional OECD growth ranking and robust export performance offer long-term investment appeal, near-term volatility driven by won weakness, foreign capital outflows, and semiconductor sector uncertainty demands caution. Investors should monitor the June 16-17 Federal Reserve meeting and upcoming May CPI data, as US monetary policy developments will significantly influence Korean asset prices. Real estate investors face challenges from jeonse market compression and affordability pressures, though price-capped apartment units in the Seoul metropolitan area show resilience through significantly higher competition rates. Technology sector investors should watch the AI data center development and global semiconductor cycle closely, as these mega-trends will ultimately determine Korea's economic trajectory beyond the immediate volatility.
headline: Korean Economy Shines as GDP Growth Tops OECD Rankings
